title: The Lamb on Mount Zion and the Harvest of the Earth
summary: John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who bear his and his Father's name, singing a new song. Three angels then proclaim the eternal gospel, announce the fall of Babylon, and warn that those who worship the beast will drink the wine of God's wrath, while a voice from heaven declares the dead who die in the Lord at rest. The chapter ends with two harvests: one like a Son of Man reaps the earth, and an angel gathers the grapes of the earth into the winepress of God's wrath.
story: Chapter 13 showed the beasts at the height of their power, marking the world and making war on the saints. Chapter 14 answers with a counter-vision. Instead of the beast on the seashore, the Lamb stands on Zion; instead of the beast's mark, his people bear his Father's name. Then the chapter announces, in brief, what the rest of the book will show at length: the gospel going to all nations, Babylon's fall (chapters 17 and 18), the judgment of the beast's worshipers, and the final harvest (chapters 19 and 20). It is a preview of the ending, set here to steady the churches before the seven bowls of chapters 15 and 16.
historical:
Babylon is named here for the first time. The historical Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the first temple in 587 or 586 BC and carried Judah into exile, and it had fallen to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. By the first century Babylon had become a code name among Jews and Christians for the power that oppressed God's people; 1 Peter 5:13 sends greetings from she who is in Babylon, widely taken as Rome. Most interpreters read Revelation's Babylon, the great city that makes the nations drunk, as Rome in the first instance. Some preterists read it as Jerusalem, which had rejected the Messiah. Futurists often expect a final world city or system, and idealists read it as the recurring seductive city of human pride.

The 144,000 described as virgins who were not defiled with women have been read in several ways, but almost no one takes the chapter as condemning marriage, which the New Testament honors (Hebrews 13:4). The imagery was also pointed in a setting where the worship of many gods was intertwined with festival banquets and sexual license, which Revelation connects in its letters to the churches (2:14, 20).
cultural:
Mount Zion is the hill of Jerusalem where God set his king in Psalm 2:6, and where Joel promised deliverance for those who call on the LORD (Joel 2:32). Firstfruits were the first portion of the harvest, offered to God as belonging to him and as a pledge of the rest (Leviticus 23:10). Israel's soldiers kept themselves from sexual relations while on campaign (Deuteronomy 23:9-10; 1 Samuel 21:5), and the prophets called idolatry adultery and faithfulness virginity (Jeremiah 3; 2 Corinthians 11:2). Both backgrounds may shape the description of the 144,000.

The cry “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” echoes Isaiah 21:9 and Jeremiah 51:7-8, where Babylon made the nations drunk with her wine. The cup of God's wrath is an old prophetic image (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15). Undiluted wine was notable because wine was normally mixed with water. Fire and sulfur recall the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:24), and smoke rising forever comes from Isaiah 34:9-10's oracle against Edom. The harvest with a sickle and the treading of the winepress come from Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:1-6. Grapes were trodden by foot in stone vats, and the juice ran out red. The 1,600 stadia (a stadion was about 185 meters) is roughly 300 kilometers, which some note is about the length of the land of Israel; the number is also four squared times a hundred.
literary: The chapter is built in seven scenes, some marked by and I saw, others by a new angel: the Lamb and the 144,000 (vv. 1-5), three angels with three messages (vv. 6-11), a call for perseverance and a beatitude (vv. 12-13), and two harvests (vv. 14-20). The three angels move from invitation to announcement to warning. The second of Revelation's seven beatitudes (sayings beginning Blessed) appears in verse 13 and is confirmed by the Spirit. The two harvests are debated. Many read both as judgment, one of grain and one of grapes, as in Joel 3:13. Others read the first, reaped by one like a Son of Man, as the gathering of the righteous (compare Mark 4:29; Matthew 13:30) and the second, thrown into the winepress, as the judgment of the wicked. The images build toward the vision of Christ treading the winepress in 19:15.

outline.t: The Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
Third angel: the fate of the beast's worshipers; a call to endure
The dead who die in the Lord
The harvest of the earth by one like a Son of Man
The grape harvest and the winepress of God's wrath

doctrines.note: An angel carries the eternal gospel to every nation, tribe, tongue, and people, calling them to fear God, give him glory, and worship the creator. Even at the edge of judgment, the book extends invitation.

Those who worship the beast will drink the cup of God's wrath. Revelation holds that allegiance has consequences, and that the final judgment is carried out in the presence of the Lamb, not apart from him.
The dead who die in the Lord rest from their labors, and their deeds follow them. Death for the believer is not loss but rest, and faithfulness is not forgotten.

words.note: Aparchē, firstfruits, the first part of the harvest dedicated to God. Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20) and James calls believers a kind of firstfruits (James 1:18). The 144,000 are offered to God as his own, a pledge of the full harvest to come.

Thumos, passion, fury, wrath. Babylon makes the nations drink the wine of the passion (thumos) of her immorality, and those who drink it will drink the wine of God's thumos. The wordplay makes judgment fit the sin: the cup offered is the cup returned.

Hupomonē, perseverance, enduring under pressure. As in 13:10, the call to the saints is not to calculate or to fight but to keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus, remaining faithful under the beast's pressure.

Drepanon, a sickle, the curved blade used for harvest. It appears seven times in this passage. Jesus used harvest as a picture of the end of the age (Matthew 13:39), and the sickle marks this as the moment when what has grown is gathered.

christ: The chapter opens with the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, the place of the Messiah's enthronement in Psalm 2, surrounded by his redeemed. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, a picture of discipleship. The seated figure on the cloud, “One like the Son of Man,” comes from Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive everlasting dominion, and it was Jesus' own favored title for himself (Mark 14:62). The golden crown marks him as king. The chapter holds together the Lamb who redeems and the Son of Man who judges: the same Jesus who was slain for people from every nation is the one to whom judgment is given (John 5:22-27).

hard.q: Does verse 11 teach that the wicked are tormented forever?
hard.a:
This verse is central in the debate over the nature of final judgment, and Christians who share the same creeds have read it differently. The traditional view, held by the great majority of the church through history, reads verses 10 and 11 as describing conscious punishment without end, and points to 20:10, where the devil, the beast, and the false prophet are tormented day and night forever. A second view, often called conditional immortality or annihilationism, and held by a minority of evangelical and other scholars, argues that the final judgment ends in destruction rather than endless torment. Its defenders note that the image of smoke rising forever comes from Isaiah 34:9-10, where the smoke of Edom's ruin rises forever yet wild animals later inhabit the land, so the image speaks of permanent and irreversible ruin; they also stress the Bible's language of death and destruction for the wicked. Defenders of the traditional view reply that no rest day or night describes ongoing experience.

The church's confession on either reading is that final judgment is real, just, and permanent, carried out in the presence of the Lamb who died for sinners. The warning is given so that it will not have to be fulfilled for its hearers: the same chapter opens with the eternal gospel offered to every nation.

questions: The 144,000 follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Where might following him lead you that you would rather not go?
The first angel calls every nation to fear God and give him glory. How does it change the tone of this chapter to see the gospel announced before the harvest?
Those who die in the Lord rest, and their deeds follow them. What would you want to follow you?
